Name: Linux
SDKs & notable repos: The entire kernel is the SDK. Subsystem docs under Documentation/; `elixir.bootlin.com` for fast cross-referenced browsing
Downloadable / offline docs: Kernel docs build to HTML/PDF from source (`make htmldocs`); full tree cloneable
Notes: Read `docs.kernel.org/process/howto.html` before anything else if you intend to contribute.

Name: FreeBSD
SDKs & notable repos: Unified base system — kernel and userland in one tree, which makes it far easier to study than Linux
Downloadable / offline docs: Handbook and Developer's Handbook as HTML/PDF/EPUB
Notes: The Handbook is the best-written OS documentation in existence. Worth reading even if you never run FreeBSD.

Name: OpenBSD
SDKs & notable repos: pledge/unveil, OpenSSH, LibreSSL, pf all originate here
Downloadable / offline docs: man pages are the documentation, and they are complete
Notes: Famous for correctness-first culture. The man pages are normative, not supplementary.

Name: NetBSD
SDKs & notable repos: rump kernels — run kernel components in userspace, a genuinely unusual capability
Notes: Best codebase for studying portability across architectures.

Name: illumos
SDKs & notable repos: DTrace, ZFS and Zones originated in this lineage
Notes: The Solaris heritage. DTrace's architecture is still worth studying.

Name: Haiku
SDKs & notable repos: BeOS-compatible, pervasively multithreaded design
Notes: A modern, complete, readable OS that isn't Unix. Valuable precisely for that.

Name: ReactOS
SDKs & notable repos: Open reimplementation of the Windows NT kernel and userland
Notes: The most accessible way to understand NT internals.

Name: Redox
SDKs & notable repos: Microkernel OS written in Rust, with its own userland
Notes: Shows what a memory-safe systems language does to OS design.

Name: Fuchsia (Zircon)
SDKs & notable repos: Capability-based microkernel; component framework; FIDL IPC
Notes: Google's from-scratch OS. The capability model documentation is excellent.

Name: XNU (macOS/iOS)
SDKs & notable repos: Mach + BSD hybrid; source released per OS version
Downloadable / offline docs: Source only — Apple publishes little kernel prose
Notes: Source is released but undocumented. Read it alongside the Mach papers.

Name: Windows
SDKs & notable repos: WDK, WinDbg, ETW, Sysinternals
Downloadable / offline docs: Microsoft Learn supports offline/PDF export per section
Notes: No source, but the driver and Win32 documentation is extensive and precise.

Name: Zephyr
SDKs & notable repos: West build tool, device tree, Kconfig; 750+ supported boards
Downloadable / offline docs: Sphinx docs per release; repo cloneable
Notes: The Linux Foundation RTOS. Device-tree-driven, which makes it feel like a small Linux.

Name: FreeRTOS
SDKs & notable repos: Tiny kernel, very wide MCU support; AWS-maintained
Downloadable / offline docs: Free PDF reference manual and the 'Mastering FreeRTOS' book
Notes: The kernel is a few thousand lines — read the scheduler directly.

Name: Apache NuttX
SDKs & notable repos: POSIX-compliant RTOS — you can run near-standard code on a microcontroller
Notes: Unusual: real POSIX semantics at tiny scale.

Name: seL4
SDKs & notable repos: Formally verified microkernel; machine-checked proofs of functional correctness
Notes: The only general-purpose kernel with a full functional-correctness proof. The proof approach is as interesting as the kernel.

Name: xv6-riscv
SDKs & notable repos: A complete Unix-like kernel in about 10,000 lines of C
Downloadable / offline docs: The xv6 book (free PDF) — the companion text that explains every subsystem
Notes: The single best artefact in OS education. Read the book and the source side by side.

Category: 3. Teaching kernels — read and modify these
Name: Pintos
SDKs & notable repos: Skeleton kernel with four staged projects: threads, user programs, VM, filesystem
Notes: Harder than xv6 because you implement the missing parts yourself.

Category: 3. Teaching kernels — read and modify these
Name: OS/161
SDKs & notable repos: Teaching OS with a full graded assignment sequence and public autograder
Notes: The most complete free OS course-in-a-box.

Category: 3. Teaching kernels — read and modify these
Name: MINIX 3
SDKs & notable repos: Microkernel designed for teaching, with Tanenbaum's textbook behind it
Notes: Historically important — the system Linux was written in reaction to.

Category: 3. Teaching kernels — read and modify these
Name: Writing an OS in Rust
SDKs & notable repos: Incremental blog-series kernel: bootloader, interrupts, paging, async
Downloadable / offline docs: Online, with full source per post
Notes: The best modern from-scratch tutorial, in any language.

Category: 3. Teaching kernels — read and modify these
Name: The Little OS Book
SDKs & notable repos: Short x86 kernel-from-scratch guide
Notes: Minimal and honest about scope.

Category: 3. Teaching kernels — read and modify these
Name: OSDev Wiki
SDKs & notable repos: The community reference for bare-metal development: boot, A20, GDT, paging, ACPI
Notes: Uneven in quality but irreplaceable. 403s to bots; fine in a browser.

Name: POSIX / Single UNIX Specification
SDKs & notable repos: The normative definition of Unix system and shell interfaces
Downloadable / offline docs: Free to read online in full
Notes: When documentation and implementation disagree, this is the arbiter.

Name: Linux man-pages
SDKs & notable repos: Section 2 (syscalls) and 7 (overviews) are the real Linux API documentation
Downloadable / offline docs: Installable via package manager; browsable online
Notes: The section 7 overview pages (`man 7 signal`, `man 7 capabilities`) are underused and excellent.

Name: OCI Runtime Specification
SDKs & notable repos: Defines what a container actually is, in terms of namespaces and cgroups
Notes: Short. Read it and container magic disappears.

Name: runc
SDKs & notable repos: The reference OCI runtime — where the namespace and cgroup calls actually happen
Notes: The bridge between 'container' and 'Linux kernel feature'.

Name: containerd
SDKs & notable repos: Container runtime used by Docker and Kubernetes

Name: eBPF / bpftrace
SDKs & notable repos: High-level tracing language over eBPF; one-liners that replace whole tools
Notes: The modern way to ask the kernel arbitrary questions.

Name: Brendan Gregg's site
SDKs & notable repos: Flame graphs, USE method, systems performance methodology
Notes: If you measure Linux performance, this is the reference body of work.

Name: FlameGraph
SDKs & notable repos: The visualization that made profiling legible

Name: perf
SDKs & notable repos: Kernel-integrated profiler and counter interface

Name: strace
SDKs & notable repos: Syscall tracer — still the fastest way to find out what a program actually does

Name: Valgrind
SDKs & notable repos: Memory error detection, cachegrind, callgrind

Name: GDB
SDKs & notable repos: Including kernel debugging via QEMU + gdbstub
Downloadable / offline docs: Full manual online and as PDF/info
Notes: Debugging a kernel under QEMU with GDB is the highest-leverage skill in OS work.

Name: LWN.net
SDKs & notable repos: Kernel development reporting of exceptional technical quality
Downloadable / offline docs: Subscriber articles become free after a week
Notes: The best single source for what is actually changing in Linux and why.

Name: Elixir cross-referencer
SDKs & notable repos: Browse any kernel version with symbol cross-referencing
Notes: Far faster than grepping a local tree when you're orienting.

Name: KernelNewbies
SDKs & notable repos: Per-release changelogs and first-patch guidance

Name: Linux From Scratch
SDKs & notable repos: Build a working distribution from source, step by step
Notes: Teaches how a userland is assembled, which kernel study alone will not.

Name: Linux Kernel Module Programming Guide
SDKs & notable repos: Actively maintained modern rewrite of the classic LKMPG
Downloadable / offline docs: Online and as PDF from the repo
Notes: The fastest path from C programmer to writing a loadable kernel module.

Name: Linux Inside
SDKs & notable repos: A guided walk through the kernel source from the boot process onward
Notes: Reads the actual source with you, line by line. Occasionally dated, still the best tour available.

Name: Linux Kernel Labs
SDKs & notable repos: University lab series on device drivers, memory management and filesystems with QEMU setups
Notes: Structured exercises with working skeletons — rare for kernel-level teaching material.

Name: Bootlin training materials
SDKs & notable repos: Full slide decks and lab manuals for embedded Linux, kernel and driver development
Downloadable / offline docs: Hundreds of pages of PDF slides, Creative Commons licensed
Notes: Commercial training material given away free. Among the best embedded Linux resources in existence.

Name: syzkaller
SDKs & notable repos: Coverage-guided kernel fuzzer; syzbot reports bugs continuously upstream
Notes: Reading syzbot reports is an education in how kernels actually fail.

Name: Rust for Linux
SDKs & notable repos: Rust support merged into the mainline kernel; abstractions and example drivers
Notes: The most consequential change to kernel development practice in decades. Still evolving quickly.

Name: Tock OS
SDKs & notable repos: Embedded OS in Rust with memory-isolated applications on microcontrollers
Notes: Shows what type-safety buys you at the embedded level, where you have no MMU to fall back on.

Name: Hubris
SDKs & notable repos: Oxide Computer’s embedded OS, with an unusually candid design rationale
Notes: The documentation explains why each design decision was made, including the rejected alternatives.

Name: Asahi Linux
SDKs & notable repos: Apple Silicon reverse engineering and Linux port
Notes: Currently better documentation of Apple Silicon internals than Apple provides.

Name: arXiv
SDKs & notable repos: Preprints across all of CS; most systems, ML and PL work appears here before publication
Downloadable / offline docs: Every paper is a free PDF. Bulk access documented at https://info.arxiv.org/help/bulk_data/index.html; a full-text API at export.arxiv.org
Notes: Not peer-reviewed. Treat an arXiv-only paper as a claim, not a result — but it is where you will read almost everything first.

Name: ar5iv
SDKs & notable repos: Renders any arXiv paper as responsive HTML instead of PDF
Notes: Makes papers readable on a phone and searchable in-page. Underused.

Name: alphaXiv
SDKs & notable repos: arXiv papers with a public comment and discussion layer
Notes: Useful when a paper is contested — the discussion often contains the critique you were looking for.

Name: Semantic Scholar
SDKs & notable repos: 200M+ papers with citation graph, influential-citation scoring and TLDR summaries
Downloadable / offline docs: Free Graph API (https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api), bulk datasets available on request
Notes: The best free citation graph. 'Highly influential citations' is a genuinely useful filter for finding what actually mattered.

Name: OpenAlex
SDKs & notable repos: Fully open catalogue of works, authors, venues and institutions; successor to Microsoft Academic Graph
Downloadable / offline docs: Entirely free API with no key required; complete database snapshots downloadable
Notes: The only large-scale bibliographic database that is open all the way down, including bulk snapshots.

Name: DBLP
SDKs & notable repos: Authoritative CS bibliography — complete author and venue listings
Notes: The fastest way to find everything a given researcher has published, and to see a conference's full programme by year.

Name: OpenReview
SDKs & notable repos: ICLR, NeurIPS, COLM and dozens of other venues — papers plus the full review threads
Notes: Reading the reviews and author rebuttals teaches you how the field evaluates work. Nothing else exposes this.

Name: CORE
SDKs & notable repos: Aggregates 300M+ open-access papers from repositories worldwide
Notes: Good for finding the green open-access copy when a publisher's version is paywalled.

Name: Unpaywall
SDKs & notable repos: Finds legal free copies of paywalled papers via DOI
Notes: Legal, author-deposited copies only. Install the extension and most paywalls simply stop appearing.

Name: Papers We Love
SDKs & notable repos: A curated, categorised repository of classic CS papers with local meetup talks
Downloadable / offline docs: Repo cloneable; many PDFs mirrored in-repo
Notes: The best starting point if you do not yet know which papers matter in a subfield.

Name: The Morning Paper (archive)
SDKs & notable repos: Adrian Colyer's daily paper summaries, 2014-2021
Notes: No longer updated, but the back catalogue of ~1000 summarised papers is one of the great free CS resources.

Name: USENIX Proceedings
SDKs & notable repos: OSDI, SOSP (co-published), NSDI, ATC, FAST, Security — the core systems venues

Notes: USENIX made everything open access years before the rest of the field. If a systems paper exists, check here first.

Name: ACM Digital Library

Name: IEEE Xplore
